theory.intro: Most figures need more than one rule. Work one angle at a time, using whichever triangle, quadrilateral or polygon property fits. The interior and exterior angles of polygons often give you the first fact.
facts: In a triangle the angle sum is $180^{\circ}$, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$.
In a quadrilateral the angle sum is $360^{\circ}$, opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and every angle of a rectangle or square is $90^{\circ}$.
In a regular $n$-gon each interior angle is $\frac{180(n-2)}{n}$ and each exterior angle is $\frac{360}{n}$.
A diagonal of a regular polygon usually creates an isosceles triangle.
Angles on a straight line add to $180^{\circ}$, angles at a point add to $360^{\circ}$, and vertically opposite angles are equal.
On parallel lines, alternate angles are equal and co-interior angles add to $180^{\circ}$.
Write a reason after every line: a value with no reason is not a finished answer.
Drawing an auxiliary line, such as a diagonal or a parallel through a point, is often the key move.
steps: Mark every angle you can find, each with a reason.
Use a triangle, quadrilateral or polygon in which only one thing is unknown.
Repeat until you reach the required angle.

foundation.solution_text:
$\angle ABC=120^{\circ}$ (interior angle of a regular hexagon)
$AB=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles (sides of a regular hexagon)
$x=(180^{\circ}-120^{\circ})\div2$
$=30^{\circ}$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle)

$\angle ABC=108^{\circ}$ (interior angle of a regular pentagon)
$AB=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles (sides of a regular pentagon)
$x=(180^{\circ}-108^{\circ})\div2$
$=36^{\circ}$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle)

$\angle$ of a regular hexagon $=120^{\circ}$
$\angle$ of a square $=90^{\circ}$
$a=360^{\circ}-120^{\circ}-90^{\circ}$
$=150^{\circ}$ (angles at a point)

$\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-115^{\circ}=65^{\circ}$ (angles on the straight line $ABD$)
$x=180^{\circ}-65^{\circ}-40^{\circ}$
$=75^{\circ}$ (angle sum of $\triangle ABC$)

$\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-74^{\circ}=106^{\circ}$ (angles on the straight line $ABE$)
$x=180^{\circ}-106^{\circ}$
$=74^{\circ}$ (co-interior angles, $AB\parallel DC$)
$y=106^{\circ}$ (opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal)

development.solution_text:
$\angle ABC=135^{\circ}$ (interior angle of a regular octagon)
$AB=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles (sides of a regular octagon)
$x=(180^{\circ}-135^{\circ})\div2$
$=22.5^{\circ}$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle)

$\angle$ of a regular pentagon $=108^{\circ}$
$\angle$ of a square $=90^{\circ}$
$b=360^{\circ}-108^{\circ}-90^{\circ}$
$=162^{\circ}$ (angles at a point)

$\angle ACD=65^{\circ}$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel DC$)
$AD=DC$, so $\triangle ADC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle DAC=\angle DCA=65^{\circ}$
$x=180^{\circ}-65^{\circ}-65^{\circ}$
$=50^{\circ}$ (angle sum of $\triangle ADC$)
